note: The builder starts from a real recipe wherever a free-to-use Carolina one exists, and says so on the page. Where none exists, the proportions are this project's own, composed to keep the ingredient order the labels print and to land on the sugar the bottles actually carry. Those are marked inference. The sugar figure under each result is computed from the quantities on screen, using 12.6 g of sugar in a tablespoon of sugar, 10 g in molasses and 3.7 g in ketchup, and it is drawn against the bottles measured for this site. A home sauce generally lands below them.

bases.name: Vinegar and pepper
bases.region: Eastern North Carolina and the Pee Dee
bases.says: Thin, clear, sharp. Nothing to thicken it and nothing to hide behind.

anchor.title: Eastern North Carolina Barbecue Sauce
anchor.note: scaled down from its ¾ gallon of vinegar; the proportions are the recipe's own

method: Stir everything together cold until the salt is gone.
Let it stand an hour at least, overnight if you can, so the pepper opens up.
Shake before it goes near the meat; it separates and is meant to.

bases.name: Lexington dip
bases.says: The eastern sauce with ketchup and a little sugar stirred in. Still thin enough to pour.

anchor.note: No free-to-use Lexington recipe exists — every pit keeps its own. These proportions follow the order the record gives: vinegar, ketchup or tomato, water, salt, pepper, a little sugar. They come out well short of the 3.5 g of sugar a tablespoon of the average bottled dip carries, which is the point: the shelf is sweeter than the pit.

method: Warm the vinegar and water enough to take the sugar and salt into solution.
Whisk in the ketchup, then the peppers, off the heat.
Let it sit until it is cool and the colour has evened out.

bases.name: Light tomato
bases.region: The Pee Dee and the upper Midlands
bases.says: Vinegar and pepper reddened with ketchup — thin, not sticky.

anchor.note: Composed the same way as the dip, with less ketchup. Like the dip, it lands under the bottles — the two light-tomato bottles on file measure about 2 g of sugar a tablespoon.

method: Stir the sugar and salt into the vinegar and water until they go.
Whisk in the ketchup and the pepper.
Stand it an hour before you use it.

bases.name: Mustard
bases.says: Yellow mustard, vinegar, sugar, pepper. The German counties' sauce.

anchor.title: Sauce for Barbecues (receipt 335)
anchor.note: Mrs. Hill's 1867 basting sauce — butter, a large spoonful of mustard, red and black pepper, salt, and vinegar 'until the sauce has a strong acid taste' — is the documented ancestor, not the modern Midlands bottle. The mustard-forward proportions here are this project's own; the butter is left out, because the modern sauce is a dressing rather than a baste. It comes out far drier than the bottles, which measure about 5.3 g of sugar a tablespoon.

method: Whisk the mustard and vinegar smooth before anything else goes in.
Add the sugar, salt and pepper and warm it gently, without boiling, until the sugar is gone.
Cool it. It thickens a little as it goes.

bases.name: Heavy tomato
bases.region: The Upstate and the western counties
bases.says: Tomato, brown sugar or molasses, vinegar, cooked down until it clings.

anchor.note: The Wikibooks sauce nearest this one is Kansas City's, a different animal, and is not used here. These proportions keep the label order the Upstate bottles print. Even cooked down it sits under their measured 5 g a tablespoon; turn the sweetness up if you want the shelf's version.

method: Put everything in a pan together and bring it to the barest simmer.
Hold it there twenty minutes, stirring, until it coats the back of a spoon.
Cool it before bottling; it thickens again cold.

bases.name: Pepper vinegar
bases.says: The bottle beside the sauce, not instead of it.

anchor.title: Pepper Vinegar
anchor.note: Mary Randolph's 1824 receipt, verbatim in the proportions she gives: a dozen ripe pods, three pints of vinegar boiled away to one quart. The pods are strained out, so the finished quart is vinegar.

ingredients.name: ripe hot peppers, stemmed and halved

method: Halve the pods and put them in the vinegar.
Boil three pints away to a quart, as Randolph has it, then strain.
Bottle it. It keeps, and it gets hotter for a week or two.
